```{r load}
library(bridges)
set.seed(42)
```

# Example data

We simulate 120 cells in which allele A of chromosome 1 undergoes BFB
cycles; chromosome 2 only acquires focal gains and losses. Real data must
have the same columns (`cell_id`, `chr`, `start`, `end`, `A`, `B`, `CN`),
with chromosome names without the `"chr"` prefix and the same bins for all
cells.

```{r data}
sim <- bridge_sim(
    chromosomes = c("1", "2"),
    bfb_allele = "1:A",
    max_cells = 500,
    subsample = 120,
    lambda = 0.75,
    bfb_prob = 0.8,
    amp_rate = 0.1,
    del_rate = 0.1
)
cna_data <- sim$cna_data
```

# Fitting the tree

`fit()` infers the phylogeny and reconstructs the ancestral profiles that
the tree-based tests below use. How it compares cells (the greedy and
BFB-aware distances), builds and roots the tree, and handles whole-genome
duplications is explained in
`vignette("modelling", package = "bridges")`.

```{r fit}
res <- fit(cna_data, chromosomes = c("1", "2"), verbose = FALSE)
```

# BFB detection on the tree

At each internal node, the reconstruction compares a greedy cost G and a
BFB cost B for the node's two children, and records $\delta = G - B$. A
node with $\delta > 0$ is BFB-like. `detect_bfb_branches()` counts the
BFB-like nodes for every chromosome and allele and runs a one-sided
binomial test against the background rate `threshold`, with
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across tests. With `fit(wgd = TRUE)`, nodes
just above a whole-genome duplication are left out.

```{r branches}
branches <- detect_bfb_branches(res, threshold = 0.005)
branches
```

Allele A of chromosome 1 should have the largest fraction of BFB-like
nodes.

`detect_bfb_branches()` counts BFB-like nodes over the whole tree, so BFB
that happened in only part of the population can be diluted by the rest.
`detect_bfb_clades()` instead scans every clade of the tree, reports the
clade where BFB-like nodes are most concentrated, and corrects for having
looked at many clades:

```{r clades}
clades <- detect_bfb_clades(res, threshold = 0.005, seed = 1)
clades[, c("chr", "allele", "p.scan", "adj.pval", "clade_bfb_nodes",
           "clade_nodes", "clade_n_cells")]
```

`plot_heatmap()` colours the branches leaving BFB-like nodes and marks
those nodes:

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 7}
plot_heatmap(
    cna_data,
    fit = res, chr = "1", allele = "A",
    chromosomes_to_plot = c("1", "2"),
    to_plot = c("A", "B"),
    branch_length = 1,
    use_raster = FALSE
)
```

`plot_bfb_signature()` shows, for each genomic segment, how many BFB-like
nodes involve it:

```{r signature, fig.height = 4}
plot_bfb_signature(res, chr_of_interest = "1", allele_of_interest = "A")
```

# BFB detection in individual cells

## Count-vectors

The second approach needs no tree. A copy-number profile along one
chromosome arm, read from the telomere towards the centromere, is reduced
to a count-vector: the copy number of each successive segment, with
deletions dropped. Whether some series of BFB cycles can produce a given
count-vector is an exact combinatorial question (Kinsella and Bafna, 2012;
Zakov, Kinsella and Bafna, 2013), answered by the `bfbtools` package.

`bfb_detect_vectors()` works on a list of count-vectors:

```{r vectors}
bfb_detect_vectors(list(
    c(6, 3, 5),
    c(14, 7, 18, 16, 9, 12),
    c(1, 1)
))
```

- `admits_bfb` is `TRUE` when the vector can be produced by BFB cycles.
- For vectors that cannot, `bfb_distance` is $-\log$ of the weight of the
  nearest BFB-compatible vector under a Poisson noise model (0 for an exact
  match).
- Every BFB cycle duplicates part of the chromosome, so vectors whose
  maximum is below `min_max_count` (default 2), like `c(1, 1)`, are
  reported as `NA` rather than as trivially compatible.
- Identical vectors are computed only once; `n_unique` reports how many
  distinct vectors were evaluated.

## From copy-number tables

`bfb_detect_batch()` extracts a count-vector for every cell, chromosome and
allele of a copy-number table and runs `bfb_detect_vectors()` on all of
them.

## Chromosome arms

Each chromosome arm has its own telomere, so a BFB pattern is read from
the end of the arm towards the centromere. In ascending genomic
coordinates the p-arm already runs telomere to centromere, but the q-arm
runs the other way. With `genome = "hg19"` or `"hg38"`, rows are assigned
to arms using the bundled `centromeres` table (`split_chr_arms()`), each arm
is analysed separately, and q-arms are reversed.

The example below places the same BFB pattern, 6-3-5 from the telomere, on
both arms of chromosome 1:

```{r arms}
arm_example <- data.frame(
    cell_id = "cell_1",
    chr = "1",
    start = c(1e6, 2e6, 3e6, 200e6, 201e6, 202e6),
    end = c(2e6, 3e6, 4e6, 201e6, 202e6, 203e6) - 1,
    A = c(6, 3, 5, 5, 3, 6)
)
bfb_detect_batch(arm_example, alleles = "A", genome = "hg19")
```

Both arms are compatible with BFB. Read as a single chromosome, the same
row would be the vector 6-3-5-5-3-6, which mixes the two arms. When data
cover both arms, always supply `genome`.

On the simulated cells:

```{r batch}
cells <- bfb_detect_batch(cna_data, alleles = c("A", "B"), genome = "hg19")
cells <- cells[!is.na(cells$admits_bfb), ]
aggregate(admits_bfb ~ chr + arm + allele, data = cells, FUN = mean)
```

The two approaches complement each other: the tree-based test uses the
relationships between cells, while the per-cell test is exact but looks
at one profile at a time.

# References

Kinsella M, Bafna V (2012). Combinatorics of the breakage-fusion-bridge
mechanism. *Journal of Computational Biology* 19(6):662-678.

Zakov S, Kinsella M, Bafna V (2013). An algorithmic approach for
breakage-fusion-bridge detection in tumor genomes. *PNAS*
110(14):5546-5551.
